item.title: What are the main events for today?
item.description:
EUROPEAN SESSION

In the European session, the main highlight was the UK labour market report. The data was a bit mixed, with unemployment falling to 4.6% and employment beating expectations, but declining payrolls and vacancies pointing to underlying weakness. Wage growth also continued to moderate, which could reinforce the central bank's view of easing inflationary pressures.

Overall, the report didn't change anything for the BoE's outlook, with markets still pricing in an 89% probability of a rate hike in December and a total of 95 bps of tightening by the end of 2027.

Looking ahead, we also get the German ZEW survey which is expected at 28.8 vs 28.1 in the prior month. The data won't change anything for the ECB at this point, so the market reaction will likely be muted. As a reminder, the market is pricing in a 91% chance of a rate hike at the next meeting and a total of 68 bps of tightening by the end of 2027. The Vice President of the ECB yesterday suggested that markets pricing in another rate hike in 2027 is not unreasonable.

AMERICAN SESSION

In the American session, we have the US retail sales, more Fedspeak and NVDA earnings after the market close. The US Retail Sales are expected at 0.1% vs 0.8% prior, while the Ex-Autos measure is seen at 0.4% vs 0.9% prior. The Control Group, which provides a cleaner indication of underlying consumer spending, is expected at 0.4% vs 0.1% prior. Retail Sales is a very volatile and coincident indicator, so it rarely changes anything for the markets. There's generally a spike, followed by a reversal. 

This week is a bit empty in terms of key economic data that could change expectations. A Fed rate hike in December is already set in stone and the only thing that markets have been debating on is how much more tightening the central bank is likely to deliver by the end of 2027. 

Lastly, we get Nvidia earnings (ticker NVDA) after the market close. The company is expected to report Q3 FY2027 revenue of approximately $108.8 billion, representing an increase of around 90% y/y. Adjusted EPS is forecast at approximately $2.47, up around 90% from the same period last year.In the previous quarter, Nvidia reported revenue of $96.2 billion and adjusted EPS of $2.22. For the current quarter, management previously guided for revenue of approximately $108 billion, putting analyst expectations broadly in line with its own outlook.

Markets will focus particularly on data entre revenue, gross margins and forward guidance, looking for evidence that hyperscaler demand for AI infrastructure remains strong. The market will also be looking for updates on the ramp-up of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin platform.

item.title: Could the internet go dark?
item.description:
Chimpanzees can choose the right tool for a task and even modify it in advance; crows drop stones into water to raise its level and reach floating food; and octopuses can unscrew jars to get to what's inside. That is called causal reasoning, something humans are particularly good at, although it can sometimes lead us down the wrong path.

For example, following recent outages in Microsoft services and a technical glitch in the U.S. air traffic control system, some interpreted these as signs of an impending digital apocalypse.

There's even a date — November 17th.

The theory goes that hackers will break into the world's biggest banks, wipe out everyone's accounts, and shut down the internet for three months, sending the world into chaos and panic. Such fears could also spill over into financial markets, affecting investor confidence and driving demand for safe-haven assets, while putting the U.S. dollar index in focus.

The good news is that there's no master switch to turn off the internet. It's a huge network of undersea cables, satellites, data centers, and telecom operators, so taking the whole thing offline is unlikely.

Still, the global network does face real threats, just not the kind these theories suggest. A much more likely scenario is a major outage caused by shared dependencies, when multiple services suddenly lose access to the same cloud provider. And we have seen this happen more than once in recent years.

One of the biggest examples was the CrowdStrike Falcon update in July 2024, which crashed around 8.5 million Windows devices worldwide, grounding flights and disrupting hospitals and banks.

Earlier, on November 8, 2023, around 10 million Optus customers in Australia lost service for roughly 12 hours after a software upgrade at one of the company's international network connections went wrong.

Another threat, and one we've already started seeing, is AI making it easier to hack systems.

In October, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model uncovered two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites worldwide, that could have allowed hackers to take control of websites, steal passwords, data, and more.

CrowdStrike has also reported an 89% jump in AI-powered attacks, while the time it takes hackers to get inside a network has hit a record low of just 27 seconds. As AI-related risks grow, technology stocks could face increased scrutiny, making Nasdaq 100 futures an important indicator of how investors assess the outlook for the tech sector.

The takeaway?

A global internet shutdown is unlikely, but AI is making cyberattacks more dangerous, meaning better data protection, backup servers, and regular backups are more important than ever.

item.title: UK September ILO unemployment rate 4.6% vs 4.7% expected
item.description:
• Prior 4.7%
  • Employment change 156k vs 136k expected
  • Prior 102k
  • Average weekly earnings +3.6% vs +3.5% 3m/y expected
  • Prior +3.7% (revised to 3.8%)
  • Average weekly earnings (ex bonus) +3.5% vs +3.6% 3m/y expected
  • Prior +3.7%
  • October payrolls change -34k
  • Prior 13k (revised to 20k)
  • Full report

The UK labour market data for September is a bit mixed, with the headline figures pointing to improving employment conditions but other indicators still pointing to some underlying weakness.

The unemployment rate fell to 4.6% from 4.7%, beating expectations of 4.7%. Employment was also stronger than expected, increasing by 156K in the three months to September, compared with 136K expected and 102K previously.

The improvement in the headline figures needs to be treated with some caution. The ONS highlighted significant differences in employment status between groups entering and leaving the survey, which partly contributed to the movements in the employment and unemployment rates.

Moreover, the October payrolls figures painted a less encouraging picture, with the number of employees on company payrolls falling by 34K, following an upwardly revised increase of 20K in September. Vacancies also continued to decline, with smaller businesses particularly affected by rising labour and operating costs.

On the wages front, there were further signs of easing inflationary pressures. Average weekly earnings excluding bonuses increased by 3.5% y/y in the three months to September, slightly below the 3.6% expected and down from 3.7% previously. Including bonuses, earnings growth slowed to 3.6% from a revised 3.8%, although this was marginally above the 3.5% consensus.

The slowdown in regular wage growth was primarily driven by weaker public sector pay growth as the impact of the timing of pay awards started to fade. Public sector regular earnings increased by 5.4% annually, compared with 3.1% in the private sector.

In real terms, regular pay growth remained modest at just 0.4% using CPI. This suggests that while nominal wage pressures are gradually easing, households are still experiencing relatively limited improvements in purchasing power.

The report doesn't change much for the Bank of England. The stronger employment and falling unemployment figures suggest that the labour market remains relatively resilient, but declining payrolls, falling vacancies and moderating regular wage growth point towards gradually weakening conditions. Nevertheless, the Bank of England will likely want to see further evidence that wage pressures are sustainably easing before becoming more confident about the inflation outlook.

The market is currently pricing in an 89% probability of a rate hike at the next meeting in December, with a total of 95 bps of tightening by the end of 2027.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Kuroda, once Japan’s great easer, says BOJ rates may need to rise above neutral
item.description:
For Japanese rates and the yen, a call for above-neutral rates from the architect of Japan’s easing era adds weight to the hawkish tail of BOJ pricing. Most economists see a terminal rate near 1.75%, and talk of 2.5% now has a high-profile backer. Kuroda no longer sets policy, so the direct effect is limited. Still, his critique of the food tax cut puts the fiscal-monetary tension in sharp relief ahead of an expected December hike. Front-end JGB yields, with the two-year near 1.88%, are most exposed to any shift toward a higher peak. Oil matters here too. Kuroda explicitly links Japan’s inflation risk to the Iran war, so a renewed energy spike would strengthen the case he describes.

---

The governor who took Japan into negative rates now says the BOJ may need to go beyond neutral. He blames imported inflation from the Iran war and a food tax cut he says will feed prices, not growth.

Summary:

  • Former BOJ Governor Haruhiko Kuroda says rates may need to rise above neutral if inflation becomes more serious.
  • He cited cost pressures from the US war with Iran, given Japan’s reliance on imported oil, materials and food.
  • The BOJ is widely expected to hike next month. Economists see a peak of 1.75%, and some see as high as 2.5%.
  • Kuroda said PM Takaichi’s planned food sales tax cut, worth about ¥10 trillion, would push up prices, not growth.
  • He described Japan’s July to September contraction as probably temporary.
  • He revealed he believed in 2016 that rates could not go much below minus 0.1%.

Former Bank of Japan Governor Haruhiko Kuroda says interest rates may need to rise above the neutral level if inflation pressures intensify, according to an interview reported by Bloomberg via The Japan Times. It is a striking message from the architect of a decade of ultra-loose policy.

Kuroda said the outlook depends entirely on inflation. If price pressures become more serious, he said, rate hikes would naturally have to speed up and could take the policy rate beyond neutral, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. He pointed to the cost pressures Japan faces from the US war with Iran, given the country’s heavy reliance on imported oil, raw materials and food.

His comments come as investors focus on how far the BOJ’s tightening cycle can run. The central bank is widely expected to raise rates next month. The median economist forecast sees the policy rate peaking at 1.75%, roughly two more hikes, though some see it reaching as high as 2.5%. About two weeks ago, the BOJ board under Governor Kazuo Ueda judged underlying inflation to be consistent with its target for the first time since the goal was set in 2013. Kuroda called that a welcome development but said the bank’s job is not done.

He also took aim at fiscal policy. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi plans to cut the sales tax on food for two years from April, a package expected to add around ¥10 trillion, or roughly $63 billion, to the economy. With unemployment at just 2.4% and the economy running at capacity, Kuroda said the tax cut would push up prices rather than growth. That would leave the BOJ no choice but to keep raising rates.

Data released on Monday showed Japan’s economy contracted in the July to September quarter, with consumer spending hit partly by unusually bad weather. Kuroda played down the figures, describing the weakness as probably temporary.

The interview also offered a rare look back. Kuroda served two terms and is the longest-serving governor in the BOJ’s history. In a book published last month, he revealed that when the bank introduced negative rates of minus 0.1% in 2016, he believed it would be difficult to cut further, despite the bank’s repeated pledges to do so if needed. Financial institutions, he said, may not have been able to absorb deeper negative rates. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Lock in yields not seen in 25 years, PIMCO urges, while calling stocks very expensive
item.description:
Coming from one of the world’s largest bond managers, a call to lock in yields for three to five years supports demand for longer-dated government and agency debt. It also leans against the steady rise in long-end yields. The message sits alongside Morgan Stanley’s view that markets are too hawkish, but against Goldman’s expectation of two more Fed hikes. That divergence is likely to keep rate volatility elevated. PIMCO’s warning on expensive equities and tight credit spreads suggests the big institutions are split on whether stocks or bonds offer the better risk-reward. Its base case links stability to the Middle East settling down within months. A longer energy shock would test that view.

---

PIMCO’s message is simple: yields this high come along about once a generation. It says investors should lock them in with high-quality bonds rather than sit in cash or chase expensive stocks and tight credit.

Summary:

  • PIMCO says bond yields are near their highest in about 25 years, driven by the Middle East energy shock and a rise in real rates.
  • A broad US bond index yields in the mid-5% range, against core inflation in the mid-2% range, giving investors a cushion missing in 2021.
  • The firm has shifted toward longer maturities and is moving up in quality, favouring government bonds, senior asset-backed securities and agency MBS.
  • It is avoiding bank loans and high yield, and sees credit spreads near historically tight levels.
  • It describes stocks as very expensive relative to earnings and real rates.
  • Its base case sees uncertainty easing once the Middle East stabilises, which it expects within several months.

PIMCO says bond yields near their highest levels in about 25 years offer investors a rare chance to lock in income for the next three to five years. It argues that high-quality fixed income now provides a cushion that was missing before the 2022 bond rout.

In an interview-style outlook published on November 16, Group Chief Investment Officer Dan Ivascyn and strategist Esteban Burbano said the surge in yields has been driven by the energy price shock from the Middle East conflict and a sharp rise in real, or inflation-adjusted, interest rates. Inflation expectations have risen far less.

The cushion is the core of their argument. A broad US bond market index now yields in the mid-5% range, against core inflation in the mid-2% range. That’s very different from early 2021, when bonds offered almost no income buffer before inflation surged and yields jumped. PIMCO noted that investors who held active income portfolios from the yield levels of late 2023 went on to earn high-single-digit returns over three years.

The firm has shifted from favouring short-term bonds to favouring longer maturities to lock in current yields, with overall duration roughly in line with the broad US bond index. Its theme is moving up in quality. It prefers global government bonds, senior asset-backed and structured securities, and US agency mortgage-backed securities, which it says offer a yield advantage over investment-grade corporate bonds. It is underweight tightly priced, lower-quality credit and is avoiding bank loans and high-yield bonds. It is holding cash in reserve for opportunities if markets are disrupted. Outside the US, it favours high-quality markets such as Australia and the UK, along with selected emerging market rates.

PIMCO was blunt on equities. It described stocks as very expensive relative to earnings and real rates, and noted that similar valuations have tended to precede weak returns. That view contrasts sharply with Morgan Stanley’s maximum overweight on global equities this week.

On cash, the authors argued that it locks in yield for only one day, and that holding cash after a large rise in rates has often proved the riskier choice. Their base case is that uncertainty lingers until the Middle East stabilises, which they expect within several months. The main risks they flag are:

  • a prolonged energy shock
  • strain on consumer lending and commercial real estate from higher real rates
  • AI overinvestment
  • US fiscal sustainability

PIMCO is moving up in quality, favouring government and agency bonds while avoiding high yield and bank loans.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgan Stanley bets on gold at $5,250, the boldest bank call with bullion near $3,875
item.description:
For gold, the Morgan Stanley call gives bulls a powerful anchor at a time when the metal is trading near a one-year low and analysts are warning of ETF selling. It doesn’t change the near-term drivers, though: the December Fed decision, Treasury yields above 5% and a dollar near its highest since April 2025 are still in control. The bank’s own forecast of a firmer dollar makes the target a deliberate contrarian call that gold can decouple from rates. The test will be whether ETF flows turn positive while the Fed is still hiking. The gap of about $600 between Morgan Stanley and Goldman shows how little consensus there is on gold’s 2027 path, so expect volatility.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold hits 1-year low near $3,830, on course for worst year since 2015 as yields bite

---

With gold near a one-year low and bearish calls mounting, Morgan Stanley has gone the other way. It sees $5,250 by late 2027 and is betting the metal can climb through the same rate and dollar headwinds that have been dragging it down.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley names gold its top commodity pick for 2027, with a target of $5,250 an ounce by the fourth quarter.
  • That’s about 36% above spot near $3,865 and the highest of the major bank forecasts.
  • Its quarterly path runs $4,850, $5,000, $5,100 and $5,250, an average of about $5,050, roughly 9% above consensus.
  • The bank cites strong demand and gold’s resilience to higher US rates and a stronger dollar.
  • UBS targets $5,000 for the same quarter, and Goldman Sachs sees $4,650 by end-2027, with a new record only in 2028.
  • Near term, gold remains under pressure from Fed hike expectations, with $3,800 the next level to watch.

Morgan Stanley has named gold its top commodity pick for 2027. It forecasts the metal will reach $5,250 an ounce by the fourth quarter of next year, roughly 36% above current levels and the highest target among the major banks.

The call is part of the bank’s 2027 cross-asset outlook. It comes with gold near $3,865, close to a one-year low and on course for its worst year since 2015. That puts Morgan Stanley firmly against the recent run of bearish analyst views as Treasury yields and the dollar climb.

The path to $5,250

Morgan Stanley’s quarterly forecasts map a steady climb through 2027. They start at $4,850 in the first quarter and rise to $5,000, $5,100 and then $5,250 by year-end, an annual average of around $5,050. That average is roughly 9% above the market consensus. The bank’s commodity team, led by strategist Amy Gower, has pointed to strong demand and gold’s resilience to higher US interest rates and a stronger dollar as reasons for its view.

That second point is the boldest part of the call. Gold has fallen this year largely because markets expect the Federal Reserve to keep raising rates, which lifts yields and the dollar. Morgan Stanley’s own 2027 outlook expects a modest dollar rally, so its target effectively assumes gold can climb through the very headwinds that have pushed it lower.

How the big banks compare

The gap between the major houses is unusually wide. UBS targets $5,000 for the fourth quarter of 2027, $250 below Morgan Stanley. Goldman Sachs, after cutting twice this month, sees $4,650 by end-2027 and does not expect a new record until 2028. Spot gold would need to rise about 20% just to reach Goldman’s target.

What would need to happen

For Morgan Stanley’s forecast to play out, investors and central banks would need to return as buyers despite higher rates. Central bank demand has been a pillar of gold’s long rally, but Poland, one of the most active buyers, has recently reached its reserve target. Flows into exchange-traded funds reversed sharply as rate expectations rose, and they would likely need to turn positive again.

The near-term picture remains difficult. Analysts have warned that ETF selling could deepen the current slide, with $3,800 the next level to watch. Morgan Stanley’s target is a view on the year ahead, not a call on the next few weeks.

item.title: More from Morgan Stanley: 8,700 S&P target and $5,250 gold lead its 2027 outlook

That counts for more on a day when chip export curbs and Goldman’s call for more Fed hikes are pulling the other way. ---

adding in more now.

---

Morgan Stanley has backed its max-overweight equity call with hard numbers. It sees 8,700 on the S&P 500, a firmer dollar and gold at $5,250, and believes cheaper valuations and AI spending can carry markets through 2027.

Summary:

  • The index’s forward P/E has fallen to 15x, the lowest since 2023, and the bank expects that headwind to ease.

Morgan Stanley has put numbers to its maximum overweight call on global equities. It has set an S&P 500 target of 8,700 for the end of 2027 and named gold as its top commodity pick, with a forecast of $5,250 an ounce.

As reported on Monday, the bank has moved to its most bullish stance on global stocks, arguing that the AI investment cycle remains intact. The fuller outlook adds the targets and cross-asset calls behind that view.

Earnings and valuations

Its equity analysts have kept their baseline AI investment projections, and they expect the question of how chips are financed to dominate the AI funding debate in 2027.

Credit and rates

The bank has raised corporate credit to equal weight, saying risk assets have cheapened enough to justify taking more risk. Because tail risks remain, it recommends pairing that exposure with quality. It prefers investment grade to high yield across regions, favours loans over high-yield bonds in the US and is neutral on data center debt. In rates, it sees market pricing as more hawkish than its economists expect. It favours German Bunds and UK gilts, and forecasts the 10-year US Treasury yield at 5% and the 10-year Bund at 3.10%.

Currencies and commodities

item.title: NZ 1-year inflation expectations jump to 2.9%, but the 2-year anchor barely moves
item.description:
For the RBNZ, the survey is mixed rather than alarming. The stable two-year reading lets policymakers argue that expectations remain anchored. The one-year jump and the higher OCR expectations show forecasters now firmly expect tightening. That supports pricing for a hike at the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement, and any pushback from the RBNZ would surprise. For the New Zealand dollar, near 0.55, higher rate expectations give some support, though the move in the two-year gauge is too small to be a strong driver on its own. The slump in house price expectations is a reminder that tighter policy is already biting. That may temper how far the RBNZ is willing to go.

---

Earlier:

  • New Zealand food prices fall 0.4% in October as RBNZ flags 3 rising global risks

---

New Zealand forecasters are bracing for higher inflation next year but still trust the RBNZ to bring it back over two years. They also expect it to raise rates to get there.

Summary:

  • One-year inflation expectations rose to 2.92% from 2.60%, and two-year expectations edged up to 2.36% from 2.34%.
  • Five-year and 10-year expectations fell, to 2.17% and 2.13%.
  • Respondents expect the OCR at 3.05% by the end of December, above the current 2.75%, and at 3.40% in a year.
  • Annual CPI inflation was 3.7% in the September quarter, still above the RBNZ’s 1% to 3% target band.
  • One-year-ahead unemployment expectations held at 5.24%, while wage expectations rose to 2.90%.
  • One-year house price inflation expectations fell to just 0.51%.

New Zealand businesses and professional forecasters lifted their near-term inflation expectations sharply in the fourth quarter, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s latest Survey of Expectations showed on Tuesday. But the two-year measure the RBNZ watches most closely barely moved.

One-year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 2.92% from 2.60%, a jump of 32 basis points. Two-year-ahead expectations edged up to 2.36% from 2.34%. Longer-term measures eased: five-year expectations fell to 2.17% from 2.31%, and the 10-year gauge slipped to 2.13% from 2.20%.

Why the two-year number matters

Policymakers focus on the two-year horizon because it roughly matches how long it takes for changes in interest rates to work through the economy. If businesses expect inflation to stay high over that period, they are more likely to build it into wages and prices, which makes inflation harder to bring down. A two-year reading close to the middle of the RBNZ’s 1% to 3% target band suggests expectations remain anchored, even though the short-term outlook has worsened.

The jump in the one-year measure probably reflects recent experience. Annual CPI inflation was 3.7% in the September quarter, down from 4.1% in the June quarter but still above the target range. The survey went into the field on 23 October, the day after those figures were released.

Rate expectations move higher

Respondents also expect higher interest rates. The mean expectation for the official cash rate at the end of the December quarter was 3.05%, above the current 2.75%. That implies an expected hike at or before the RBNZ’s next Monetary Policy Statement on 9 December. One-year-ahead OCR expectations rose to 3.40% from 3.21%.

The rest of the survey was mixed. One-year-ahead unemployment expectations held at 5.24%, one-year wage inflation expectations rose to 2.90%, and GDP growth expectations improved. House price expectations fell sharply, with house price inflation one year ahead now seen at just 0.51%.

What to watch

The firmer one-year reading combined with a stable two-year anchor gives the RBNZ room to argue that expectations are under control. But the rate expectations in the survey show that respondents believe more tightening is coming. The 9 December statement will show whether the central bank agrees. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Surplus story takes the wheel in oil for now, nudging Brent lower
item.description:
For oil, the market is choosing to price the IEA’s surplus forecast over the headlines from Hormuz. That leaves crude vulnerable to a sharp reversal if any of the recent tanker attacks is independently confirmed as a major loss. The OPEC+ capacity review and the November 29 meeting are the next policy catalysts. Higher baselines for 2027 would support the surplus case, and restraint would undercut it. The SPR at its lowest since 1982 means Washington has less room to cushion any new supply shock. That matters more if the risk premium makes a comeback.

---

Oil traders are leaning on the IEA’s surplus forecast, not the tanker attacks, for now. But the story this market tells about itself tends to follow price, and it can turn quickly.

Summary:

  • Brent slipped and WTI also fell in Asian trade on Tuesday.
  • The IEA expects the oil market to return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, as Middle East exports recover faster than demand.
  • The US-Iran risk premium hasn’t disappeared, but it is taking a back seat for now, one analyst said.
  • Attacks on tankers in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz are continuing.
  • OPEC is reviewing members’ production capacity ahead of an OPEC+ meeting on November 29 to set 2027 policy.
  • The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to its lowest since 1982.

Oil prices edged lower in Asian trade on Tuesday, Reuters reported, with Brent futures slipping just below $92 a barrel. Expectations of a looming supply surplus outweighed fresh attacks on tankers in the Gulf. US West Texas Intermediate crude also fell.

The surplus view gained traction after the International Energy Agency said on Friday that the global oil market will swing back into surplus in the fourth quarter. Middle East exports are recovering faster than global demand, despite ongoing attacks on shipping. One analyst said the market increasingly accepts that supply has caught up with demand and may soon exceed it. The analyst added that the geopolitical risk premium from the US-Iran conflict has not disappeared but is taking a back seat for now.

There are still plenty of risks in that back seat. A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was disabled by an attack near Khasab, Oman, on Monday, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency, and Iran’s navy claimed it had hit four tankers in 24 hours. Separately, China resumed stockpiling crude in October, which adds a source of demand on top of refinery consumption.

Supply policy is also in focus. OPEC held an online meeting on Monday to discuss its review of members’ maximum sustainable production capacity, an exercise that will help set OPEC+ output quotas for 2027 and beyond. The wider OPEC+ group, which includes Russia, meets on November 29 to decide its 2027 policy.

In the United States, crude stocks in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to around 276 million barrels last week, the lowest since August 1982, according to Department of Energy data. The drawdowns are part of an agreed release of 172 million barrels.

A word of caution on the surplus narrative. Market explanations tend to follow price, and they can change just as quickly. Today the story is supply catching up with demand. Tomorrow, a confirmed sinking in Hormuz, a major supply outage or a surprise from OPEC+ could put the risk premium back in the driving seat, and the commentary would shift with it. For traders, the levels and the flows usually matter more than whatever label the market attaches to them on a given day. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Two more Fed hikes, then a long pause: Goldman reads a third hot core CPI print
item.description:
A January hike is a step beyond what the market has firmly priced, so Goldman’s call leans against any rally at the front end. The two-year yield’s jump to near 4.86% shows how quickly expectations can move. For the dollar, a longer tightening cycle supports the policy divergence already weighing on currencies such as the yen and the Aussie. Gold is vulnerable too, since it has repeatedly fallen as Fed hike expectations rise rather than acting as a haven. Equities face the same pressure on valuations seen across AI names this month. The key test is whether Fed officials start to talk openly about January before the December meeting.

---

The latest jaw boning from the Fed:

  • Hammack: Economy can handle more restriction, unclear how far Fed has to go

---

Three strong core inflation readings in a row have convinced Goldman that summer’s slowdown was a blip. It now expects the Fed to hike in January as well as December before taking a long breather.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs Asset Management expects the Fed to hike in December and again in January, followed by a prolonged pause.
  • US core CPI rose 0.3% in October, an annualized pace of about 3.6%, beating expectations for a third firm reading in a row.
  • The summer’s softer prints now look temporary rather than the start of a disinflationary trend.
  • Strength was broad, spanning supercore services, housing and core goods, which makes it harder for the Fed to look through the data.
  • The two-year Treasury yield rose to around 4.86% as of November 11.
  • Further hikes are possible if inflation proves sticky, and Goldman remains cautious on US rates.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management expects the Federal Reserve to keep raising interest rates beyond December, after a third consecutive strong reading on US core inflation. It forecasts back-to-back hikes in December and January, followed by a prolonged pause.

Core consumer prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3% in October. That is an annualized pace of about 3.6% and was above market expectations. Goldman said the run of three firm prints suggests the softer readings over the summer were temporary rather than the start of a sustained slowdown in inflation. Its charts show the three-month annualized rate of core inflation climbing back to around 3.7%, and the year-on-year measure has edged higher in recent months.

What concerns the asset manager most is the breadth of the increase. Strength showed up across several categories at once. One was so-called supercore inflation, which tracks services prices excluding housing and is closely watched by the Fed as a gauge of wage-driven pressures. Housing and core goods also rose. Goldman argued that such widespread gains make it harder for policymakers to dismiss the data as noise, particularly while the labor market remains resilient.

Markets have moved in the same direction. The two-year Treasury yield, the maturity most sensitive to Fed expectations, had jumped to around 4.86% as of November 11, according to Goldman’s figures, a sharp recovery from a dip in October.

Goldman’s base case is for consecutive hikes in December and January, followed by an extended hold. It cautioned, however, that further increases could follow if inflation proves sticky. For portfolios, the firm said it remains cautious on US interest rates, citing resilient growth and inflation momentum that reinforce the Fed’s hawkish bias.

The view adds to a growing debate over how far the tightening cycle has to run. Investors will look to the next round of inflation and labor market data, and to Fed officials’ comments ahead of the December 8-9 meeting, for signs of whether a January move is gaining support inside the central bank. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan delays its first 2-year floating-rate JGB: what it says about BOJ bets
item.description:
The delay has little direct effect on JGB supply, since the floater never launched and the issuance plan is still being drafted. Its value is as a signal. The issuer itself is saying that investors see little need to hedge against BOJ tightening, which suggests front-end yields already price in a hiking path. That makes the market more sensitive to any upside surprise from the BOJ: if policy tightens faster than priced, short-dated JGBs would reprice and the case for floaters would quickly return. For the yen, the read is neutral to mildly supportive, since it confirms that rate expectations are already high. The November 26 meeting with primary dealers is the next place to watch for hints on how the fiscal 2027 plan will reshape issuance across maturities.

Newswire cut: Japan is postponing a new two-year floating-rate government bond as markets already price in BOJ hikes, sources told Reuters, reducing the appeal of a product built to shield investors from rising yields. No new launch date has been set for now.

One-line wrap: Tokyo built a bond to protect investors from BOJ rate hikes, but the bond market has already priced the hikes in. So the insurance has gone back on the shelf before it was ever sold.

Summary:

  • Japan’s Ministry of Finance is postponing a planned two-year floating-rate government bond, according to two sources.
  • Issuance had been targeted for as early as January, and no new date has been set while the ministry reassesses demand.
  • A floating-rate note’s coupon resets with market rates, which shields investors from losses when yields rise.
  • Markets increasingly price in future BOJ hikes, which reduces the bond’s value as a hedge.
  • It would have been Japan’s first short-dated floating-rate government bond. Japan has issued 15-year floaters before.
  • The decision will feed into the fiscal 2027 issuance plan, due at year-end after a November 26 meeting with dealers.

Main article: Japan’s Ministry of Finance is postponing the launch of a new two-year floating-rate government bond while it reassesses whether investor demand would hold up, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters on Tuesday. The ministry had targeted issuance as early as January but will now hold off on setting a date. The ministry was not immediately available for comment.

What is a floating-rate bond?

A conventional government bond pays a fixed coupon for its whole life. When market interest rates rise, that fixed payment becomes less attractive, and the bond’s price falls. A floating-rate note works differently. Its coupon resets periodically in line with market rates, so when rates go up, the income goes up too, and the bond’s price stays relatively stable. In effect, it is insurance against rising yields rather than a bet on them.

Why Tokyo wanted one

The ministry began preparing the product in 2024, as the Bank of Japan moved away from years of ultra-loose policy and started raising rates. The aim was to keep investors buying Japanese government debt at a time when holding fixed-rate bonds looked increasingly risky. A two-year maturity would have tied the coupon closely to the BOJ’s policy path. That would have made it Japan’s first short-dated floating-rate government security, although Japan has issued 15-year floaters in the past.

Why the appeal has faded

Insurance is most valuable when a risk is underpriced. According to the sources, bond markets have increasingly priced in future BOJ rate increases, so fixed-rate yields already compensate investors for much of the expected tightening. A floater only beats a fixed bond of the same maturity if the BOJ ends up hiking by more than the market expects. With that expectation largely built in, the hedge offers less. The ministry is no longer confident that demand would be steady enough to support regular issuance.

What it says about BOJ expectations

The delay is a quiet signal from the issuer itself that markets have caught up with the BOJ’s tightening story. Japan’s two-year yield, the maturity the floater would have matched, was trading near 1.88% early on Tuesday. At that level, investors are already being paid for a substantial part of the expected rate path without needing a floating coupon. The delay also shows how quickly conditions have shifted since 2024, when rising yields were the risk investors wanted protection from.

What to watch next

The decision will feed into Japan’s fiscal 2027 bond issuance plan, due at the end of this year after consultations with primary dealers and other market participants, including a meeting on November 26. The ministry will revisit the plan at its mid-year review in June, so the floater could return if the rate outlook changes. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: WSJ: US imposes chip export licenses on 5 countries to close China’s data center loophole
item.description:
For chip stocks, the rule adds a regulatory hit to a sector already weighed down by the Nvidia leadership turmoil. AMD and CoreWeave fell 5% or more and Nvidia about 4%. Licensing requirements in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore cloud the outlook for the region’s fast-growing data center trade, a source of demand for US chips. The TSMC provision brings Taiwan’s chip supply chain into scope, which could weigh on Asian tech names. The bigger near-term risk is Beijing’s response during Trump’s China trip this week. Retaliation or stalled trade talks would add to the pressure.

---

Earlier:

  • BlackRock keeps 5-year US equity overweight on AI conviction despite tactical caution
  • Goldman Sachs: chip stocks near 3-year valuation low even as demand outruns supply

---

Washington is closing the side door that let Chinese firms rent American AI chips through Southeast Asian data centers. The bigger surprise is that the Commerce Department’s own rule had to be written by other agencies.

Summary:

  • Shipments of advanced US chips to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil now need Commerce Department licenses, though US tech firms may get exceptions.
  • The rule aims to stop Chinese customers accessing AI computing remotely through data centers in third countries. It also restricts Chinese chip designers’ work with TSMC.
  • It takes effect immediately, with a 60-day comment period.
  • The rule was written by and at the direction of Treasury and the National Security Council, which export-control specialists called highly unusual.
  • Treasury Secretary Bessent has accused Commerce of stalling, and President Trump defended Commerce Secretary Lutnick, citing relations with China.
  • AMD and CoreWeave fell 5% or more and Nvidia closed about 4% lower.

The US Commerce Department has issued a rule requiring licenses for shipments of advanced chips from Nvidia and other US companies to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported. The aim is to stop Chinese customers from tapping AI computing power remotely through data centers in those countries.

The rule takes effect immediately, with a 60-day window for company comments, and US tech firms may be able to obtain exceptions. It would also make it harder for data center operators anywhere in the world to give Chinese companies remote access to AI chips. And it would make it harder for Chinese chip designers to work with TSMC, the world’s leading contract chipmaker.

The rule targets the network of companies that have used Nvidia chips to build data centers across Southeast Asia and rent that capacity to Chinese technology groups trying to catch up in AI. The Journal singled out Megaspeed International, a firm linked to the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive last week.

How the rule was produced is as notable as what it says. The Bureau of Industry and Security normally drafts chip-export measures. Its release said this rule had been written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council. Export-control specialists called that highly unusual. One former State Department official said it suggested Commerce had resisted the rule until the White House forced it to act.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has accused Commerce of holding up action on Megaspeed and export-control loopholes for months, adding to pressure on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Officials have said the department was wary of upsetting Beijing during trade talks. President Donald Trump defended Lutnick on Monday. He said the delay made sense to avoid a blowup at a time when relations with China are good.

Shares of AI and data center companies, including Advanced Micro Devices and CoreWeave, fell 5% or more after the announcement, and Nvidia closed around 4% lower. The timing is awkward, coming just as Trump travels to China this week with both Lutnick and Bessent. Lawmakers are also pushing for tougher chip-export rules in this year’s defense spending package. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold hits 1-year low near $3,830, on course for worst year since 2015 as yields bite
item.description:
Gold is being driven by rates and the dollar, not by geopolitics. Escalation in the Middle East works against it: higher oil feeds inflation, which feeds Fed hike expectations. That makes the December FOMC decision and US inflation data the key catalysts, and any repricing toward a 50 basis point hike would add pressure. The $3,800 area is the nearest support. A clean break would expose the metal to further ETF liquidation. For FX, gold’s slide adds to the headwinds facing the Australian dollar, which is already near its weakest levels since January.

---

Gold has given up more than 30% from January’s record as rising yields and a strong dollar outweigh its inflation-hedge appeal. Analysts warn that the next leg lower could come from ETF holders heading for the exit.

Summary:

  • Gold fell to a one-year low near $3,830 an ounce, more than 30% below January’s record of around $5,595.
  • The metal is on course for its worst year since 2015.
  • Treasury yields above 5%, a dollar near its highest since April 2025 and expectations of a December Fed hike are weighing on prices.
  • Analysts warn that ETF investors could start selling after a drop of almost 7% in a matter of days.
  • Goldman Sachs now sees gold at $4,150 by end-2026 and $4,650 by end-2027. (Goldman’s second gold forecast downgrade in a month turns its bear case into the base case)
  • Central bank buying and ETF inflows offer longer-term support. Poland has reached its reserve target, though, and demand for bars and coins has fallen.

Gold fell to a one-year low on Monday, according to a Reuters analysis. High Treasury yields, a firm US dollar and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy weighed on the metal, leaving bullion on course for its worst year since 2015.

Prices touched around $3,830 an ounce, the lowest since early October 2025 and more than 30% below January’s record of about $5,595. Spot gold was trading near $3,860 early in the Asian session on Tuesday, holding just above the closely watched $3,800 area.

The pressure is coming from rates. Markets expect the Fed to raise rates by 25 basis points in December, with a small chance of a larger move, and the 10-year Treasury yield is back above 5%. The dollar is hovering near its highest since April 2025, which makes bullion more expensive for buyers using other currencies. The US-Israeli war on Iran has pushed up oil prices and inflation. Gold is often seen as a hedge against inflation, but it tends to lose its appeal when rates are rising.

Analysts have turned more bearish as the $4,000 level gave way. Some noted that gold lost almost 7%, or around $290, in a matter of days last week. That was a faster drop than the move in rate expectations alone would suggest, and they warned that investors in exchange-traded funds could start selling into the weakness, deepening the decline. Others pointed to stress in equity markets, with Nvidia’s market value down around $1.9 trillion since early October. They said gold is often sold to raise cash in the short term.

Goldman Sachs has cut its gold forecasts twice this month and now sees the metal at $4,150 by the end of 2026 and $4,650 by the end of 2027.

The longer-term demand picture is more mixed. Physically backed gold ETFs took in 211 metric tons in the third quarter, and central banks bought 675 tons in the first nine months of the year. However, Poland, the most active official buyer, has reached its 700-ton reserve target, and demand for bars and coins has fallen sharply. China remains a steady buyer.

Some analysts argue that central bank buying and resilient ETF holdings may help limit the correction. They also say that support is unlikely to stop further short-term weakness if yields and the dollar keep rising. The $3,800 area is the next level to watch.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA minutes: 6 members saw rates “not clearly sufficient”, 3 warned of sharper downturn
item.description:
On balance the minutes lean hawkish, unsurpisngly. The majority’s view that 4.85% is “not clearly sufficient” sits awkwardly with market pricing that had all but ruled out further hikes, and it backs up Bullock’s comment this morning about upside risks. The minority’s warning of a sharper downturn sets a high bar for a December move, though. This week’s wage and jobs data, and the October CPI jump the staff flagged in advance, matter more than usual. For the Australian dollar, near 0.6730, the minutes are mildly supportive but unlikely to change the trend while policy diverges from the Fed. The minutes treat oil as the swing factor: if prices hold rather than ease by around US$30 a barrel as assumed, the inflation case for another hike strengthens.

---

Earlier

  • RBA’s Bullock says inflation risks still skewed to upside ahead of 6-3 vote minutes

---

The RBA majority hiked because 4.85% might not be enough, and the minority held back because the economy might already be cracking. That leaves the next move hostage to this week’s jobs data and the oil price.

Summary:

  • Six of nine RBA board members backed November’s hike to 4.85%, judging the cash rate “not clearly sufficient” to address upside inflation risks.
  • The majority cited strong market services inflation, high unit labour costs, broad cost pressures and a likely rise in the neutral rate.
  • Three members preferred to hold, warning the economy might be near a materially sharper downturn as unemployment rose half a point in six months.
  • Inflation forecasts assume oil falls by around US$30 a barrel over two years, which leaves significant upside risk if prices stay high.
  • Staff expect headline inflation to jump in October as last year’s energy subsidies drop out.
  • The board gave no explicit forward guidance beyond staying attentive to the data.

Most Reserve Bank of Australia board members judged that the cash rate was “not clearly sufficient” to bring inflation under control when they voted to raise it to 4.85% this month, according to minutes of the November meeting released on Tuesday. A three-member minority warned the economy might be close to a materially sharper downturn.

The minutes lay bare a board divided over the balance of risks. The six members who backed the 25 basis point increase, the fifth hike of the year, said forward-looking inflation pressures had risen and the risks to the outlook remained to the upside. They judged that the danger of leaving policy insufficiently restrictive, and allowing inflation expectations to drift higher, outweighed the risk of tightening too much.

The majority pointed to three signs that domestic capacity pressures were playing a bigger role than previously thought: strong inflation in market services, persistent growth in unit labour costs, and broad-based cost pressures reported by business contacts. Staff have revised up their estimate of the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation, which implies the labour market was tighter in 2026 than they had assessed. Members also noted that the neutral interest rate had likely risen, which makes any given cash rate less restrictive than before.

The three dissenters preferred to hold at 4.60%. They argued it was prudent to wait and assess the 100 basis points of tightening already delivered this year. They placed more weight on downside risks to growth, citing a half-percentage-point rise in unemployment over six months, the housing downturn and fragile sentiment toward investment in data centres.

The Middle East conflict featured heavily. Members noted that crude and refined fuel prices had risen 20% to 25% since August. The forecasts assume oil prices fall by around US$30 a barrel over two years, an assumption that requires some resolution of the conflict and leaves significant upside risk if prices stay high. Staff expect headline inflation to jump in October as last year’s energy subsidies drop out.

The board offered no explicit guidance, saying only that it will remain attentive to the data and do what is necessary to return inflation to target. Earlier on Tuesday, Governor Michele Bullock said inflation risks are still skewed to the upside. Wage data on Wednesday and October jobs figures on Thursday are the next tests.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6715 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US warns Americans in Europe of holiday terror risk as bomb hoaxes disrupt flights
item.description:
The alert is precautionary, and alerts like this rarely move markets on their own. The bigger point for markets is travel reliability heading into the busiest stretch of the year. US carriers are still clearing backlogs from last week’s FAA ground stop, and Monday’s United outage shows how little slack there is in airline systems. Any further disruption in Europe or the US during the Thanksgiving peak would bring airline and travel stocks into focus. The banking outages were resolved and described as technical. They’re more a reminder of operational risk than a credit or stability concern.

---

Also:

  • Iran drawing up dirty bomb options for Washington, 7 US officials say, not seen imminent

---

Washington is warning Americans to watch their step in Europe this holiday season. Back home, a week of grounded flights and frozen bank apps has shown that the systems people rely on can fail without any attacker involved.

Summary:

  • The US Embassy in Bulgaria issued a Europe-wide security alert urging Americans to stay vigilant during the holiday season.
  • It warns that terrorists, including lone actors, could target markets, transport hubs, malls and places of worship with little warning.
  • Strikes and demonstrations have become more frequent, and hoax bomb threats disrupted flights in numerous European countries in November.
  • Americans are advised to monitor local news, check with airlines, avoid demonstrations and enroll in the State Department’s STEP alert program.
  • In the US, an FAA ground stop, a United Airlines outage and online banking problems at major lenders caused disruption in recent days.
  • No agency or company has linked the US incidents to a cyberattack or a foreign actor.

The US Embassy in Bulgaria has issued a Europe-wide security alert urging American citizens to stay vigilant over the holiday season. It warns that terrorists, including lone actors, may strike with little or no warning, and that disruptions to travel and daily life remain possible across the continent.

The alert, dated November 16, says large gatherings and public events could be a target for terrorist groups and criminals. It singles out tourist locations such as markets, transport hubs, shopping malls and places of worship, and urges extra caution at holiday festivals and other crowded events.

On disruption, the embassy notes that strikes and demonstrations have become more frequent in recent months. It also says hoax bomb threats targeted civil aviation in numerous European countries in November, disrupting flights. Americans are advised to:

  • monitor local news and check with their airline for disruptions
  • avoid demonstrations and areas with heavy police activity
  • keep a low profile
  • enroll in the State Department’s Smart Traveler Enrollment Program for security updates

The warning comes after a run of disruption on the US side of the Atlantic. A nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop on Friday halted departures for several hours and led to around 10,000 cancellations. The government blamed a communications failure during equipment work. On Monday, United Airlines suffered a short-lived systemwide technology outage. The same day, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and other major lenders reported problems accessing online banking.

No agency or company has tied any of those US incidents to a cyberattack or a foreign actor. The FAA said its investigation found no sign of an attack, and United and Chase both said their problems were technical rather than cyber-related. Given Trump's wars I'd be sceptical of these glib explanantions. Regardless, the cluster has highlighted how exposed travel and payments are to technical failures at a busy time of year.

The timing matters for travellers. US airlines expect close to 29 million passengers over the Thanksgiving period from November 20 to 30. Europe’s holiday season brings the large markets and crowds the embassy alert focuses on. For now the advice is precautionary, and the alert does not cite a specific threat. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China resumes crude stockpiling, leaving room for fuel exports at 3 times prewar margins
item.description:
For crude, China’s return to stockpiling adds a source of demand alongside refinery consumption. That supports import levels even while runs are soft, and helps cushion prices against weaker demand elsewhere. The bigger lever is in products. With refineries running below 80% and diesel margins near triple their prewar level, more export quotas from Beijing could send significant volumes of fuel into Asian markets and narrow those margins. For now the signal points the other way: diesel exports are falling and November tracking is weaker. The tightness in middle distillates looks set to persist unless policy changes.

---

China has come through the Hormuz shock with its oil reserves intact and is rebuilding again. It also has plenty of idle refining capacity, so whether diesel margins stay this high depends largely on Beijing’s export quotas.

Summary:

  • China added close to 490,000 bpd of crude to its stockpiles in October, reversing a draw of around 530,000 bpd in September.
  • Crude imports rose to about 9.9 million bpd, the highest since March, while refinery runs slipped to around 13.7 million bpd.
  • Over the first 10 months of 2026, China has still added about 270,000 bpd to its inventories despite the disruption from the Iran war.
  • Fuel exports fell to about 5.2 million tons in October, and diesel exports dropped to around 310,000 bpd from a near three-year high in September.
  • Refineries are running at less than 80% of capacity, so there’s scope to increase exports.
  • The Singapore gasoil margin is near $59 a barrel, almost three times its prewar level.

China resumed stockpiling crude oil in October for the first time since July, as imports recovered and refinery processing stayed soft, according to a very good piece by Reuters columnist Clyde Russell. That gives Beijing room to raise fuel exports if it chooses to.

Russell calculates from official data that refiners processed close to 490,000 barrels per day less in October than the crude available to them from imports and domestic production. China doesn’t disclose flows into or out of its strategic and commercial reserves, but the gap between available supply and refinery runs gives an estimate. October’s surplus reversed a draw of around 530,000 bpd in September.

Crude imports rose to about 9.9 million bpd, up more than 9% from September and the highest since March. Domestic output was around 4.3 million bpd. Refinery throughput slipped about 2% to roughly 13.7 million bpd.

Since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, China has drawn on its inventories in May, June, August and September, with only a small build in July. Over the first 10 months of the year, however, it has still added around 270,000 bpd to stockpiles, Russell notes. Strong builds before the war and October’s rebound have offset the drawdowns. In other words, China has come through the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the early months of the conflict without running down its reserves.

Lower refinery runs have also cut fuel exports, which fell to about 5.2 million metric tons in October from around 7.2 million in September. Exports depend on government quotas, not market forces. Refiners were told to curb shipments early in the conflict to protect domestic supply, before the restrictions were eased so they could capture strong margins. Diesel exports reached about 500,000 bpd in September, the most in nearly three years. They fell to around 310,000 bpd in October, and early November tracking points lower again.

With China’s refining system running at less than 80% of capacity, there is ample room to raise output. The incentive is clear: the Singapore gasoil margin, the benchmark for diesel, ended Monday at around $59 a barrel. That is nearly three times the roughly $21 it stood at the day before the war began. Whether Beijing issues more export quotas will decide if that spare capacity reaches global fuel markets. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA’s Bullock says inflation risks still skewed to upside ahead of 6-3 vote minutes
item.description:
Bullock’s comment pushes back modestly against market pricing that has all but ruled out a December hike. It could offer the Australian dollar some support after it fell this week to its lowest level since late January. One line on a panel is unlikely to shift pricing on its own, so the minutes are the bigger test. Any sign that the majority on the board saw a real chance of further tightening would firm up the hawkish reading of Bullock’s remarks. If the minutes play up how close the vote was, front-end rates may decide the governor’s comment is a hedge, not a signal.

-

Minutes preview here:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 17, 2026: RBA minutes, plus Bullock

-

Bullock says inflation risks are still tilted higher. That reminds markets that a split board doesn’t mean the RBA is done, just as the minutes are due to show how close the debate was.

Summary:

  • RBA Governor Michele Bullock says inflation risks remain skewed to the upside.
  • She made the remarks at a panel in Sydney, shortly before the release of the November meeting minutes.
  • The RBA raised its cash rate to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth hike this year and the highest level since 2008, in a 6-3 vote.
  • Markets have priced out nearly all chance of a December rate rise.
  • The minutes are expected to show how the board weighed inflation risks against a slowing economy.
  • Wage data on Wednesday and October jobs figures on Thursday round out the week.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said on Tuesday that the risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside, Reuters reported. Her remarks come shortly before the release of minutes from the central bank’s November meeting.

Speaking on a panel at the ASIC Annual Forum in Sydney, Bullock said the board’s current view is that inflation risks are still skewed higher. The comment was brief, but its timing matters. Since the November decision, markets have priced out nearly all chance of a December rate rise. Her words suggest the board is not yet ready to declare its tightening campaign over.

The RBA lifted its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth increase this year and the highest level since 2008. The vote was unusually split: six board members backed the hike and three preferred to hold at 4.60%. That division led many analysts to conclude the bank is close to the end of its cycle.

The minutes, due at 11.30am Sydney time (0030 GMT, 7.30pm ET on Monday), should shed more light on that debate. Analysts will look at how the board weighed inflation risks against a slowing economy, whether the three dissenters judged policy already restrictive enough, and how high the bar now is for a further move. The RBA’s own assessment puts the cash rate slightly above the top of its range of neutral rate estimates. Its forecasts have inflation staying above 3% until late 2027.

Bullock’s warning about upside risks sits alongside that restrictive stance. The board may judge that rates are high enough for now, while still wanting to keep the option of another hike open if inflation does not ease as expected.

The domestic calendar is busy for the rest of the week. Third-quarter wage price data is due on Wednesday and October employment figures on Thursday, when unemployment is expected to hold at 4.7%. Firm readings on either would test the market’s conviction that the RBA has finished hiking. 

Bullock heading out of the office to buy half a cup of coffee.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran drawing up dirty bomb options for Washington, 7 US officials say, not seen imminent
item.description:
For oil, the report adds to the escalation risks around a conflict that is already disrupting Hormuz shipping. The planning is described as optional rather than imminent, though, so it adds to tail risk more than to near-term supply pressure. The more market-relevant point is the regional source’s warning that hardliners who benefit from the war could try to wreck talks over the coming weeks. That keeps the outlook for a deal to reopen the strait fragile. A US homeland incident is a low-probability event with severe consequences. It would probably hit risk assets broadly, and more as a shock to risk appetite than as a direct supply story for crude.

---

US officials say Iran has drawn up specific options for a dirty bomb or chemical attack on Washington. It is not seen as imminent, but it shows how far Tehran’s incentive to escalate has grown under US pressure.

Summary:

  • New US intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans that could target senior administration officials in Washington with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon.
  • Officials see the planning as Iran building options, not as a sign of an imminent attack, although the intelligence reportedly includes specific locations and targets.
  • The White House says there are no credible threats to the homeland. Iran rejected the chemical weapons allegations as fabricated.
  • Threats from Iran led the Secret Service to move Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent into military housing last week.
  • Separate intelligence suggests Iran could use chemical weapons against US troops in the Middle East.
  • Talks to end the US blockade and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled, and the next few weeks are seen as critical.

New US intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans that could target senior Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, CNN reported, citing seven US officials. Sources familiar with the intelligence described the planning as an effort by Tehran to give itself options, not a sign that an attack is imminent.

Even so, two of the sources said the plotting picked up by US agencies has been very specific, including locations and targets. Officials have held several meetings over the past week on contingency plans to counter it. They remain divided over whether Iran has the capability or the people in place to carry out such a plot, or the intent to try.

The White House said the US is monitoring all potential threats but that there are currently no credible threats to the homeland. Iran’s mission to the United Nations rejected what it called false and fabricated allegations, saying Tehran considers the use of chemical weapons illegitimate under any circumstances. It did not directly address the dirty bomb intelligence.

US officials see the planning as a sign that Iran is more willing to escalate as it comes under intense pressure from US strikes and an economic blockade. One source put it this way: Iran’s capability has not changed, but its incentive has. According to the report, threats from Iran also led the Secret Service to move Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent into military housing last week.

A dirty bomb wraps radioactive material around a conventional explosive and is very different from a nuclear weapon. Experts say casualties would most likely come from the blast itself, though contamination could make areas unusable. Officials are separately monitoring intelligence that Iran could use chemical weapons against US troops in the Middle East. Several said troops lack adequate protective equipment or training.

The threats come as talks to end the US blockade and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled. A regional source said the next several weeks will be critical for any agreement, and warned that hardliners who have benefited from the war could try to play spoiler. One US official said Iran understands the retaliation it would face if it used such weapons. That calculation could shift, however, if Tehran comes to see the regime’s survival as at stake.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock keeps 5-year US equity overweight on AI conviction despite tactical caution
item.description:
BlackRock’s split view separates long-term allocation from short-term positioning. That gives investors a framework for holding US equities through AI-driven volatility, not chasing or dumping them. Its higher interest rate assumptions and its shift to neutral on developed-market government bonds suggest higher yields are starting to attract long-term buyers. The stronger overweight in inflation-linked bonds points to lasting inflation risk from supply constraints, including energy. Upcoming inflation data from Japan and the euro zone will show whether those energy costs are spreading into broader prices.

---

Earlier:

  • Goldman Sachs: chip stocks near 3-year valuation low even as demand outruns supply

--- BlackRock is staying cautious on US stocks in the short term, but it is backing them for five years and more. Its bet is that AI adoption, not today’s winners or today’s earnings, will drive returns.

Summary:

  • BlackRock’s long-term conviction in AI underpins its strategic overweight in US equities over five years or longer, despite a tactical downgrade last month.
  • The view rests on AI’s improving capabilities and wider adoption, not on current earnings or market leaders.
  • Health care, IT, tech and financials are seen as having the strongest long-term earnings prospects.
  • Risks include overcapacity, squeezed supplier profits and adoption bottlenecks. The Shiller CAPE is around 41x, near dot-com highs, while the forward P/E of around 19x relies on strong earnings growth.
  • Competition for capital has led BlackRock to raise its rate expectations, and it sees policy rates staying higher for longer.
  • It has moved to neutral on developed-market government bonds and strengthened its overweight in inflation-linked bonds.

BlackRock says its long-term conviction in the AI transformation continues to underpin its strategic overweight in US equities, even though near-term risks justify a more cautious tactical stance. The world’s largest asset manager downgraded US stocks on a tactical basis last month. Its latest capital market assumptions, however, reinforce the overweight over a horizon of five years or longer.

The distinction matters. BlackRock says its longer-term view rests on AI’s improving capabilities and wider adoption over time, not on today’s earnings growth or on current market leaders staying on top. Its starting-point scenario explicitly assumes valuations will decline and does not rely on a permanent growth breakout. Even so, broader AI adoption could lift productivity, profit margins and earnings. It sees health care, IT, tech and financials as offering the strongest longer-term earnings prospects.

The near-term caution reflects genuine uncertainty over how the AI buildout develops relative to demand. Falling computing costs could squeeze suppliers’ profits, while bottlenecks could slow adoption. Overcapacity is a risk, and the companies building AI infrastructure could see earnings slow before the businesses using it see meaningful gains. On valuations, the measure matters. The S&P 500’s Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio, which uses 10 years of inflation-adjusted earnings, stands at around 41 times. That is not far below its dot-com era peak in the mid-40s. The 12-month forward multiple, at around 19 times, looks far less stretched, but only because investors expect strong earnings growth.

Funding the buildout is another theme. Companies financing AI investment are competing with heavily borrowing governments for the same pool of savings, which has prompted BlackRock to raise its interest rate expectations. It expects central bank policy rates to stay higher for longer, reflecting a higher neutral rate. It argues, though, that stronger growth and earnings can coexist with higher borrowing costs.

That repricing has made bonds more attractive. For the first time since 2020, BlackRock is taking a more constructive view on duration. It has moved to neutral on developed-market government bonds and strengthened its overweight in inflation-linked bonds. It cautions, however, that government bonds are no longer the reliable diversifiers they once were, because persistent inflation limits how far central banks can cut.

In the near term, BlackRock is watching fresh inflation data from Japan and the euro zone for signs of how higher energy costs are feeding into price pressures.

The S&P 500’s Shiller CAPE is near dot-com era highs, but the forward P/E looks far less stretched because it relies on expected earnings growth. Source: BlackRock Investment Institute, LSEG Datastream, November 2026.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran says 4th tanker hit in 24 hours as UKMTO reports Hormuz attack near Oman
item.description:
For oil, an attack in the narrowest part of the Strait of Hormuz hits the main export route for Gulf crude directly. That supports the risk premium even before any supply loss is confirmed. Crude has recently held back from reacting to unverified Iranian claims, so independent confirmation of multiple strikes is the trigger to watch for a sharper move. Higher war-risk insurance premiums and owners rerouting or delaying transits would tighten effective supply even if no cargo is lost. The US force-protection build-up suggests Washington is not expecting a quick de-escalation.

---

An attack in the narrowest part of Hormuz has left a tanker disabled and on fire. Iran says it has now hit four in a day, and the US is pouring concrete for a long stay.

Summary:

  • A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was disabled by an attack about 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at 1900 GMT on Monday.
  • The attack caused an engine room fire. The crew are reported safe, and damage and environmental impact are not yet known.
  • Iran’s navy says it has hit four oil tankers in the past 24 hours. The link to this incident is not confirmed.
  • Tehran claimed over the weekend that a supertanker sank after hitting a mine, which remains unverified.
  • The US Army is seeking 17 concrete bunkers for bases in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon within 45 days, citing risks to troops from Iranian fire.
  • A third US carrier strike group has arrived in the region.

A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was disabled by an attack on Monday that left it with an engine room fire, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency. Iran’s navy claimed it had now hit four oil tankers in the past 24 hours.

UKMTO said it received a third-party report of the incident about 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, on Oman’s Musandam peninsula, at 1900 GMT (2 pm ET). The crew were reported safe, but the extent of the damage and any environmental impact were not yet known. The agency advised vessels to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity while authorities investigate.

The Iranian navy’s announcement of a fourth tanker strike appears to relate to the same incident. That link has not been independently confirmed, and UKMTO did not identify the vessel or say who carried out the attack. Over the weekend, Tehran also claimed that a supertanker had sunk after hitting a mine, a claim that has yet to be verified.

Khasab sits on the southern side of the strait’s narrowest stretch, where the inbound and outbound shipping lanes run close to the Omani coast. An attack there goes to the heart of the main export route for Gulf crude.

The escalation at sea comes as Washington prepares for a longer confrontation. The US Army is seeking to build 17 reinforced concrete bunkers at bases in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon within 45 days. The bunkers will replace converted shipping containers that the Army says leave soldiers at risk from Iranian missile and drone fire. A third US aircraft carrier strike group has also reportedly arrived in the region, joining two already deployed.

Taken together, the tanker strikes and the US build-up in protection for its forces point to a conflict that both sides are preparing to sustain rather than wind down. For shipping, the immediate questions are whether the latest vessel can be identified and whether independent reports bear out Iran’s count of four strikes. Also watch how insurers and owners respond to a fresh attack so close to Oman’s coast. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
